# Leafy greens

<section class="hmi-quick-read" id="leafy-greens-quick-read" data-hmi-quick-read aria-labelledby="leafy-greens-quick-read-label"><div class="hmi-quick-read-label" id="leafy-greens-quick-read-label">Quick read</div>

Spinach carries the most cadmium of the common leafy greens and head cabbage among the least; lead is usually low in monitored retail leaves but rises sharply near mining, industry, roads and contaminated irrigation water.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Naser HM, Rahman MZ, Sultana S, Quddus MA, Hossain MA · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Heavy metal accumulation in leafy vegetables grown in industrial areas under varying levels of pollution</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bangladesh Journal of Agricultural Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

<ul>
<li>
<strong>Metals of concern:</strong>

Cadmium decides most leafy-green questions; lead matters near pollution sources; arsenic is high in some aquatic leaves.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM) · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009">Scientific Opinion of the Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain on a request from the European Commission on cadmium in food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">The EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">The First Hong Kong Total Diet Study: Inorganic Arsenic</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Centre for Food Safety, Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Main drivers:</strong>

Leaf type, growing site and irrigation water, then surface dust that washing can remove.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adhikari S, Struwig M · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Concentrations and health risks of selected elements in leafy vegetables: a comparison between roadside open-air markets and large stores in Johannesburg, South Africa</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Not reported</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
<li>
<strong>Practical framing:</strong>

Ask for lot cadmium and lead results by leaf on a fresh-weight basis, with the growing site.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels|8]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">European Commission · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/915 of 25 April 2023 on maximum levels for certain contaminants in food and repealing Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Official Journal of the European Union</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/eu-2023-915-contaminants-maximum-levels">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</li>
</ul>
</section>

## Leafy greens overview

<a id="hmi-ing-004"></a>
<a id="which-contamination-concerns-are-supported-for-this-ingredient-and-its-defined-forms"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-005"></a>

<a id="hmi-ing-006"></a>
<a id="which-evidence-gaps-most-limit-those-decisions"></a>

Cadmium is the metal that most often decides a leafy-green question, and the leaf type matters more than any other single factor in the monitoring data.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Across more than 2,200 WHO GEMS/Food spinach results the median was about 41 µg/kg fresh weight, against 19–20 µg/kg for leaf lettuce, 11–12 µg/kg for head lettuce and 2–4 µg/kg for head cabbage.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> The FDA Total Diet Study found the same order in US market composites from 2018 to 2020: spinach 200, leaf lettuce 57, iceberg lettuce 27 and cabbage 5.1 µg/kg as medians.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> European monitoring summarised by EFSA gave spinach a mean of 61.5 µg/kg and other leafy vegetables 23.1 µg/kg, with 3.9% of spinach samples above the EU limit.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009|4]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">EFSA Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain (CONTAM) · 2009</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009">Scientific Opinion of the Panel on Contaminants in the Food Chain on a request from the European Commission on cadmium in food</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">The EFSA Journal</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/efsa-cadmium-contam-2009">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Lead is usually low in routinely monitored retail leaves.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS composites were below a 4 µg/kg reporting limit, and EFSA’s European leafy-vegetable median was 10 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span <a id="hmi-ing-001"></a>

<div class="hmi-analyte-explorer" id="hmi-occurrence-leafy-greens" data-analyte-explorer data-compact-intro="true" data-source-summaries="true"><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure" data-explorer-context><summary data-open-context aria-haspopup="dialog" aria-controls="hmi-occurrence-leafy-greens-drawer">Comparison methods and scope</summary><div data-explorer-context-content>

<p>Each row is one statistic a source reports for one leaf, subgroup and metal; a mean, median and range from the same samples are separate rows. Ratings place a reported mean, median or sample result against a pooled HMI reference for the same leaf and basis (fresh or dry weight) built from every compatible sampling family. Same-study comparisons set a site or irrigation group against its own control or study total. Held rows failed a check against their own paper and are shown but not compared.</p>

Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>WHO GEMS/Food</td><td>1</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for amaranth leaves (cooked) on a fresh weight basis from every compatible sampling family in the evidence ledger: WHO GEMS/Food region-by-year medians (random sampling only), FDA Total Diet Study composites, per-sample results printed by individual surveys and published subgroup medians. Each family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations, and fresh-weight and dry-weight results are never converted into each other.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>An evidence-library reference for one leaf and basis, not a probability sample of any market. This is the only compatible family in the completed leafy-greens ledger for this leaf, analyte and basis; it cannot represent other markets. GEMS/Food regions are reporting regions, not growing origins. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" class="internal" data-slug="sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants" data-no-cite-meta>WHO GEMS/Food</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. Counts describe evidence units, not independent studies or certainty.</p><div class="hmi-drawer-table"><table><thead><tr><th scope="col">Contributing family</th><th scope="col">Reference units</th><th scope="col">Weight</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Martin-Leon et al. 2023</td><td>1</td><td>100%</td></tr></tbody></table></div><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Methods</p><p>HMI pools subgroup medians for watercress on a fresh weight basis from every compatible sampling family in the evidence ledger: WHO GEMS/Food region-by-year medians (random sampling only), FDA Total Diet Study composites, per-sample results printed by individual surveys and published subgroup medians. Each family has equal total weight. Non-detects stay as zero-to-limit intervals, so quartiles carry lower and upper bounds. Means, ranges and maxima never enter as observations, and fresh-weight and dry-weight results are never converted into each other.</p><p>Inverse weighted empirical CDF; midpoint at exact cumulative-weight boundaries. At least four reference units and a definitely positive Q1–Q3 spread are required. This is a display eligibility rule, not statistical validation.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Limitations</p><p>An evidence-library reference for one leaf and basis, not a probability sample of any market. This is the only compatible family in the completed leafy-greens ledger for this leaf, analyte and basis; it cannot represent other markets. GEMS/Food regions are reporting regions, not growing origins. A position is descriptive concentration, not a safety or compliance judgment.</p><p class="hmi-drawer-section-title" role="heading" aria-level="3">Admitted source families</p><ul><li><a href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements" class="internal" data-slug="sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements" data-no-cite-meta>Martin-Leon et al. 2023</a></li></ul><details class="hmi-drawer-disclosure"><summary>Reference version and interpretation</summary><p>Frozen evidence selection: 2026-10-22. <a id="sources-and-contamination-pathways"></a>
## How contamination reaches leafy greens

<a id="hmi-ing-010"></a>
<a id="what-evidence-supports-root-uptake-surface-deposition-feed-transfer-or-other-biological-pathways"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-011"></a>
<a id="what-contamination-can-arise-from-agricultural-inputs-harvesting-processing-equipment-or-packaging"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-012"></a>
<a id="which-source-attribution-claims-are-measured-modelled-inferred-or-unresolved"></a>

Leaves take metals up from soil and irrigation water, and cadmium moves into leaves more readily than lead.<sup class="cite">[[sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Naser HM, Rahman MZ, Sultana S, Quddus MA, Hossain MA · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Heavy metal accumulation in leafy vegetables grown in industrial areas under varying levels of pollution</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bangladesh Journal of Agricultural Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N&#39;guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Water</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Gazipur, Bangladesh, spinach leaves from a highly polluted industrial area carried 5,970 µg/kg lead and 1,020 µg/kg cadmium dry weight, against 1,160 and 430 µg/kg on a low-pollution research field.<sup class="cite">[[sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals|3]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Naser HM, Rahman MZ, Sultana S, Quddus MA, Hossain MA · 2018</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Heavy metal accumulation in leafy vegetables grown in industrial areas under varying levels of pollution</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bangladesh Journal of Agricultural Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In a greenhouse trial, irrigating with water containing 500 µg/L arsenic raised spinach leaf arsenic from 1.05 to 6.57 µg/g dry matter.<sup class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N&#39;guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Water</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Dust and air deposition add a surface load. Near coal-fired power plants in China, water spinach carried 86.7 µg/kg mercury fresh weight at 1 km and 23.9 µg/kg at 10 km, against 0.85 µg/kg in grocery-store leaves, and rinsing removed 19–63% of the mercury.<sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in vegetables, grains and soils from areas surrounding coal-fired power plants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Kale grown on urban farms in Baltimore averaged 130 µg/kg lead fresh weight against 10 µg/kg on rural farms nearby.<sup class="cite">[[sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland|17]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Kim BF, Lupolt SN, Santo RE, Bachman G, Zhu X, Yang T, Fukagawa NK, Richardson ML, Green C, Phillips KM, Nachman KE · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Nutrients and non-essential metals in darkibor kale grown at urban and rural farms: a pilot study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">PLOS ONE</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kim2024-metals-kale-urban-rural-maryland">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Unwashed coriander from a Johannesburg roadside market carried 191.9 mg/kg cadmium dry weight against 6.6 mg/kg once washed.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adhikari S, Struwig M · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Concentrations and health risks of selected elements in leafy vegetables: a comparison between roadside open-air markets and large stores in Johannesburg, South Africa</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Not reported</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Inputs and land use also shape levels. Phosphate fertilisers raised lettuce cadmium by up to 91% in a Chinese greenhouse field trial, while farmyard manure lowered cadmium in cabbage and lettuce compared with mineral fertiliser in a long-term English trial.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rempelos2023-vegetable-organic-conventional-metals|19]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Leonidas Rempelos, Marcin Baranski, Enas Khalid Sufar, Jenny Gilroy, Peter Shotton, Halima Leifert, Dominika Srednicka-Tober, Gultekin Hasanaliyeva, Eduardo A. S. Rosa, Jana Hajslova, Vera Schulzova, Ismail Cakmak, Levent Ozturk, Kirsten Brandt, Chris Seal, Juan Wang, Christoph Schmidt, Carlo Leifert · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rempelos2023-vegetable-organic-conventional-metals">Effect of Climatic Conditions, and Agronomic Practices Used in Organic and Conventional Crop Production on Yield and Nutritional Composition Parameters in Potato, Cabbage, Lettuce and Onion; Results from the Long-Term NFSC-Trials</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Agronomy</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rempelos2023-vegetable-organic-conventional-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/zhang2024-lettuce-cadmium-greenhouse-amendments|20]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jun&#39;an Zhang, Yingjun Hao, Guangsen Xiong, Quanzhong Tang, Xiwang Tang · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/zhang2024-lettuce-cadmium-greenhouse-amendments">Impact of Physical Interventions, Phosphorus Fertilization, and the Utilization of Soil Amendments on the Absorption of Cadmium by Lettuce Grown in a Solar-Powered Greenhouse</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Biology</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/zhang2024-lettuce-cadmium-greenhouse-amendments">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Manures raised spinach lead from 0.11 to 0.50–0.75 mg/kg in a Turkish field trial.<sup class="cite">[[sources/authors2022-compared-to-the-chemical-fertilizer-in-organic-fertilizer|21]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Unknown authors · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/authors2022-compared-to-the-chemical-fertilizer-in-organic-fertilizer">compared to the chemical fertilizer. In organic fertilizer applications, heavy metal contents such as arsenic, chrome, cobalt, and nickel were found to</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Peer-reviewed article</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/authors2022-compared-to-the-chemical-fertilizer-in-organic-fertilizer">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Mining areas raised mercury in Houttuynia leaves to 260 µg/kg dry weight against 40 µg/kg elsewhere, and lead in chard from Spanish mining-town gardens to 698 µg/kg against 118 µg/kg from a city market.<sup class="cite">[[sources/rossini-oliva2024-urban-garden-vegetables-spain|10]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Rossini-Oliva S, López Nuñez R · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/rossini-oliva2024-urban-garden-vegetables-spain">Is it healthy urban agriculture? Human exposure to potentially toxic elements in urban gardens from Andalusia, Spain</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Environmental Science and Pollution Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/rossini-oliva2024-urban-garden-vegetables-spain">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china|22]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Wang Q, Li Z, Feng X, Wang A, Li X, Wang D · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china">Mercury accumulation in vegetable Houttuynia cordata Thunb. from two different geological areas in southwest China and implications for human consumption</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Scientific Reports 11:1470</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/wang2021-houttuynia-mercury-china">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Boada, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja, Octavio P. Luzardo · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Evaluation of essential, toxic and potentially toxic elements in leafy vegetables grown in the Canary Islands</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Iceberg lettuce was lowest for lead (2.0 µg/kg), arsenic (0.5 µg/kg) and aluminium (1,581 µg/kg) in Gran Canaria, and FDA detected lead in none of 27 iceberg or cabbage composites.<sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Veronica Martin-Leon, Carmen Rubio, Angel Rodriguez-Hernandez, Manuel Zumbado, Andrea Acosta-Dacal, Luis Alberto Henriquez-Hernandez, Luis D. <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-leaves-measured-lowest-in-arsenic" data-anchor="which-leaves-measured-lowest-in-arsenic" data-question="Which leaves measured lowest in arsenic?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which leaves measured lowest in arsenic?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In Gran Canaria supermarkets, iceberg (0.5 µg/kg) and romaine lettuce (1.6 µg/kg) had the lowest total arsenic and lamb’s lettuce the highest (18.9 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Veronica Martin-Leon, Carmen Rubio, Angel Rodriguez-Hernandez, Manuel Zumbado, Andrea Acosta-Dacal, Luis Alberto Henriquez-Hernandez, Luis D. Boada, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja, Octavio P. Luzardo · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Evaluation of essential, toxic and potentially toxic elements in leafy vegetables grown in the Canary Islands</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Hong Kong, inorganic arsenic was not detected in European cabbage or lettuce, while water spinach averaged 74 µg/kg.<sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic|5]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety FEHD HKSAR · 2012</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">The First Hong Kong Total Diet Study: Inorganic Arsenic</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Centre for Food Safety, Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/cfs2012-hktds-inorganic-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Near contaminated irrigation in Gazipur, the aquatic leaf helencha carried 1.85–2.02 mg/kg arsenic dry weight.<sup class="cite">[[sources/ahmed2017-bangladesh-vegetable-arsenic|24]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Ahmed M., Kurosawa K. · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/ahmed2017-bangladesh-vegetable-arsenic">Arsenic Contamination of Water-Soil-Crop System in an Industrial Area of Bangladesh</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">International Journal of Environment</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/ahmed2017-bangladesh-vegetable-arsenic">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="which-leaves-were-lowest-in-nickel-and-aluminium" data-anchor="which-leaves-were-lowest-in-nickel-and-aluminium" data-question="Which leaves were lowest in nickel and aluminium?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Which leaves were lowest in nickel and aluminium?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

In Gran Canaria, watercress (33 µg/kg) and romaine lettuce (39 µg/kg) had the lowest nickel and spinach the highest (86 µg/kg), while aluminium ranged from 1,581 µg/kg in iceberg lettuce to 41,947 µg/kg in spinach.<sup class="cite">[[sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Veronica Martin-Leon, Carmen Rubio, Angel Rodriguez-Hernandez, Manuel Zumbado, Andrea Acosta-Dacal, Luis Alberto Henriquez-Hernandez, Luis D. Boada, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja, Octavio P. Luzardo · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Evaluation of essential, toxic and potentially toxic elements in leafy vegetables grown in the Canary Islands</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> In Hong Kong, Chinese cabbage (200 µg/kg) and European cabbage and lettuce (320 µg/kg) were lowest in aluminium and Chinese spinach highest (35,000 µg/kg).<sup class="cite">[[sources/cfs2013-hktds-metallic-contaminants|16]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Centre for Food Safety (Hong Kong) · 2013</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/cfs2013-hktds-metallic-contaminants">The First Hong Kong Total Diet Study: Metallic Contaminants</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Centre for Food Safety, Food and Environmental Hygiene Department, Government of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/cfs2013-hktds-metallic-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>
</details>

Struwig M · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Concentrations and health risks of selected elements in leafy vegetables: a comparison between roadside open-air markets and large stores in Johannesburg, South Africa</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Not reported</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|25]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Washing halves of the same Johannesburg roadside purchases lowered the group mean cadmium from 51.5 to 6.8 mg/kg and nickel from 199 to 8 mg/kg dry weight, yet the washed leaves stayed above supermarket leaves for cadmium.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Adhikari S, Struwig M · 2024</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Concentrations and health risks of selected elements in leafy vegetables: a comparison between roadside open-air markets and large stores in Johannesburg, South Africa</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Not reported</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> A 10% vinegar soak lowered lead in market lettuce from 155 to 95 µg/kg fresh weight but left farm lettuce unchanged (73.3 against 73.1 µg/kg), consistent with removal of surface lead only.<sup class="cite">[[sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing|25]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Bora FD, Bunea A, Pop SR, Banita SI, Dusa DS, Chira A, Bunea CI · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" Romania</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Horticulturae</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/bora2022-heavy-metals-fruits-vegetables-romania-vinegar-washing">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

Cooking acts differently on different metals and leaves. Boiling in clean water removed 55–69% of the arsenic from amaranth but only 3–31% from spinach, while boiling market spinach in water containing 1,000 µg/L arsenic raised it from 0.01 to 0.75 µg/g fresh mass.<sup class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, Bretzler A, N&#39;guessan ND, Tihe SFK, Lalanne F · 2021</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Uptake of Arsenic by Irrigated Vegetables and Cooked Food Products in Burkina Faso</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Frontiers in Water</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Cooking with coconut milk or oil generally lowered the in-vitro bioaccessible fraction of nickel, cadmium, chromium and lead in Sri Lankan leaves, but not in every case, and bioaccessibility is not the total concentration.<sup class="cite">[[sources/kananke2026-sri-lanka-leaf-bioaccessibility|26]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Thilini Kananke, Jagath Wansapala, Anil Gunarathne · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/kananke2026-sri-lanka-leaf-bioaccessibility">Bioaccessibility of Heavy Metals in Raw and Processed Alternanthera sessilis and Centella asiatica: An In vitro Study</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nature Environment and Pollution Technology25(1):D1830</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/kananke2026-sri-lanka-leaf-bioaccessibility">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Frozen, canned and fermented leaves are reported separately in GEMS/Food; sauerkraut, for example, had a lead median of 13–14 µg/kg, which is not a measure of what fermentation does to a given cabbage.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

## Controls for leafy greens

<a id="hmi-ing-019"></a>
<a id="which-prevention-mitigation-or-remediation-measures-have-been-evaluated-for-this-ingredient"></a>
<a id="hmi-ing-020"></a>

→</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/zhang2024-lettuce-cadmium-greenhouse-amendments|20]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Jun&#39;an <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="why-do-some-studies-report-extreme-values" data-anchor="why-do-some-studies-report-extreme-values" data-question="Why do some studies report extreme values?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>Why do some studies report extreme values?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Some extreme values do not survive a check against their own papers. In a Dhaka study every detected lead value was below the method’s own detection limit, and in a Yuyao study every mustard mean was below the crop detection limits printed in the same paper.<sup Leafy greens are a modest but real share of dietary cadmium and lead.<sup class="cite">[[sources/efsa2012-cadmium-dietary-exposure-europe|39]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span Exposure depends on how much is eaten as much as on concentration. A Southern California food-frequency survey found a mean intake of 33.6 g of leafy greens a day, and JECFA estimated that leafy vegetables gave less than 5% of the tolerable cadmium intake in every GEMS/Food region it assessed in 2006.<sup class="cite">[[sources/masri2025-toxicant-foods-california|43]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Masri S, Nasla S, Payán DD, Wu J · 2025</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/masri2025-toxicant-foods-california">Assessing Dietary Consumption of Toxicant-Laden Foods and Beverages by Age and Ethnicity in California: Implications for Proposition 65</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Nutrients</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/masri2025-toxicant-foods-california">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/jecfa-64th-cadmium-tin-2006|44]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives · 2006</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/jecfa-64th-cadmium-tin-2006">Evaluation of certain food contaminants — Sixty-fourth report of the Joint FAO/WHO Expert Committee on Food Additives</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">WHO Technical Report Series 930 (Sixty-fourth meeting of JECFA, Rome, 8-17 February 2005)</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/jecfa-64th-cadmium-tin-2006">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> No source in the ledger measured metals in finished leafy products together with the leaves that went into them.

<a id="universal-faqs"></a>
## Leafy greens FAQs

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="what-heavy-metals-have-been-measured-in-leafy-greens" data-anchor="what-heavy-metals-have-been-measured-in-leafy-greens" data-question="What heavy metals have been measured in leafy greens?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>What heavy metals have been measured in leafy greens?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Cadmium and lead are measured most often, and cadmium is the one most often found at levels that matter, especially in spinach.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup> Studies also report total and inorganic arsenic, mercury, nickel, chromium, aluminium, tin and uranium; most mercury and arsenic results in monitored retail leaves are near or below detection.<sup class="cite">[[sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants|1]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">World Health Organization · 2026</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">GEMS/Food Contaminants database heavy-metal exports</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">GEMS/Food Contamination Monitoring and Assessment Programme</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/who-gemsfood-heavy-metal-contaminants">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020|2]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">U.S. Food and Drug Administration · 2022</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">FY2018-FY2020 TDS Elements Analytical Results</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">FDA Total Diet Study</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/fda2022-tds-elements-fy2018-fy2020">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements|15]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Veronica Martin-Leon, Carmen Rubio, Angel Rodriguez-Hernandez, Manuel Zumbado, Andrea Acosta-Dacal, Luis Alberto Henriquez-Hernandez, Luis D. Boada, Maria del Mar Travieso-Aja, Octavio P. Luzardo · 2023</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Evaluation of essential, toxic and potentially toxic elements in leafy vegetables grown in the Canary Islands</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Toxics</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/martin-leon2023-canary-leafy-vegetables-elements">Read source →</a></span></span></sup>

</div>

<details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-leafy-greens" data-anchor="how-do-heavy-metals-get-into-leafy-greens" data-question="How do heavy metals get into leafy greens?">
<summary><span class="mk" aria-hidden="true"></span>How do heavy metals get into leafy greens?</summary>
<div class="ans" data-hmi-faq-answer="1">

Through roots from soil and irrigation water, and on the leaf surface from dust and air deposition.<sup class="cite">[[sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals|3]]<span href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Heavy metal accumulation in leafy vegetables grown in industrial areas under varying levels of pollution</a></span><span class="cite-card-body"><span class="cite-card-journal">Bangladesh Journal of Agricultural Research</span><a class="cite-card-review" href="../sources/naser2018-leafy-vegetables-bangladesh-metals">Read source →</a></span></span></sup><sup class="cite">[[sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains|6]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Li R, Wu H, Ding J, Fu W, Gan L, Li Y · 2017</span><a class="cite-card-title" href="../sources/li2017-mercury-coal-power-plants-vegetables-grains">Mercury pollution in <details class="qa" data-hmi-faq="1" id="can-leafy-greens-become-contaminated-after-harvest" data-anchor="can-leafy-greens-become-contaminated-after-harvest" data-question="Can leafy greens become contaminated after harvest?">

Yes, through dust, handling and cooking water.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite">[[sources/clair-caliot2021-arsenic-irrigated-vegetables-burkina|14]]<span class="cite-card"><span class="cite-card-head"><span class="cite-card-authors">Clair-Caliot G, Marks SJ, Hug SJ, boiling spinach in arsenic-contaminated water raised its arsenic from 0.01 to 0.75 µg/g.<sup class="cite">[[sources/adhikari2024-leafy-vegetables-johannesburg|7]]<span class="cite-card"><span
